newsitem.title: USA: G24 calls for more funds, better terms for debtors.
newsitem.headline: G24 calls for more funds, better terms for debtors.

text.p: The Group of 24 developing nations on Sunday called for more funds and more flexible terms for a new international plan to ease the debt burden of the world's poorest countries.

The chairman of the group of African, Asian and Latin American nations, Venezuelan Central Bank President Antonio Casas Gonzalez, said the G24 appreciated the debt relief initiative undertaken by the IMF and the World Bank.

"There is, nevertheless, a profound concern that the resources available for this facility do not appear at the moment enough to address countries' needs," Casas told a news conference after a meeting of G24 ministers.
The developing nations also believe that the application of the Highly Indebted Poor Countries Initiative (HIPC) should be sped up and its rules for eligibility made more flexible.

The HIPC aims to reward poor countries that are carrying out tough economic reforms by providing them with debt relief. Up to 25 countries, most in Africa, are expected to benefit from the plan, which could cost creditors up to $7.7 billion.
But critics, complaining about rules which could hold up the implementation of the plan for up to three years for some states, say the deal may kick in too late to be of much use.

In a communique issued after their meeting, the G24 warned that "prolonged delays in dealing with the debt overhang (of the poorest nations) will undermine the effectiveness of the initiative ... and erode domestic political support".
Noting that bilateral commitments to the HIPC remained "inadequate", the developing countries urged donor nations to provide more financial resources for the initiative.
The communique added that the G24 ministers had considered the sale of a portion of the IMF's gold reserves as a "valuable supplement to bilateral contributions".
Uganda became on Wednesday the first country to clinch a HIPC deal, under which it stands to cut its $3.4 billion debt by one fifth starting next April.
The G24's gathering took place during the International Monetary Fund's and the World Bank's joint spring meeting in Washington.
